lines.trans: Max, the dining hall is full of people again.
Yes, our evening ended very successfully.
Still, changes always happen unexpectedly.
You are right, life constantly changes around us.
Sometimes we get something completely different.

words.gloss: to receive, to get; to earn

lines.trans: We get not what we wanted before.

words.gloss: to receive, to get; to earn

lines.trans: But often everything turns out even better.

words.gloss: to turn out, develop, take shape

lines.trans: Sometimes we realize that we were right.
And our old friends remain by our side.
And sometimes we arrive back at the starting point.

All changes in life lead to the better!

lines.trans: The main thing is not to lose faith and hope.
The main thing is to believe in all changes.
All changes in life lead to the better!
All changes in life lead to the better!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

бывать.gloss: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit

meanings.en: to happen, to exist, there can be
meanings.note: 3rd person бывает = there is / can be
Secondary conversational sense ('to visit, to be at') (часто бывать где-то) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'faith, belief' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The main thing is not to lose faith.

examples.text: Главное — не терять веру и надежду.
examples.trans: The main thing is not to lose faith and hope.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to believe', forming an aspectual pair with 'поверить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to believe in') (верить в + accusative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Go on, tell her. Nina doesn't believe it.

meanings.en: to lead, to guide, to drive
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to lead', forming an aspectual pair with 'повести'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Вы как маленькая себя ведёте = You're behaving like a little girl

examples.trans: You're behaving like a little girl.

examples.text: Лидия Алексеевна, успокойтесь, пожалуйста! Вы как маленькая себя ведёте.
examples.trans: Lydia Alexeyevna, calm down, please! You're behaving like a little girl.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
до вечера = until the evening; вечером = in the evening
Secondary conversational sense ('party, evening event') (e.g. a school evening) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'around' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: She was running after me (around me).
She circled around me like a shark.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.en: after all, still, all the same
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'ё-таки').

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'main' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('the main thing') (neuter главное, used as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The main thing is, don't worry.
The most important thing is the people.

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Conversational Russian particle ('even') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.

Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'кончиться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to end', forming an aspectual pair with 'заканчиваться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.
деньги закончились = the money ran out

examples.text: Всё, выборы закончились. Тебя начальник ждёт.
examples.trans: That's it, the election is over. Your boss is waiting for you.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('living room') (regional/colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.en: sometimes, from time to time, occasionally
meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'sometimes'.

examples.trans: Sometimes a person makes astonishing discoveries.

examples.text: Иногда наши победы бывают слишком странными.
examples.trans: Sometimes our victories turn out too strange.

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'ходный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('initial, starting, baseline').

examples.trans: We returned to the starting point.

examples.text: А бывает, мы приходим в исходную точку.
examples.trans: And sometimes we arrive back at the starting point.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'better'.
лучший в мире = the best in the world
Secondary conversational sense ('better') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты мне даёшь пятьсот рублей, а я выхожу и покупаю тебе лучшую приставку в мире.
examples.trans: You give me five hundred roubles, and I get out and buy you the best console in the world.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to change', forming an aspectual pair with 'поменяться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: Да, люди вокруг меняются к лучшему.
examples.trans: Yes, people around are changing for the better.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'дежда'). Common feminine noun meaning 'hope' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Главное — не терять веру и надежду.
examples.trans: The main thing is not to lose faith and hope.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
это неожиданно = this is unexpected

examples.text: Это неожиданно, но ваш торт не такой плохой.
examples.trans: This is unexpected, but your cake isn't so bad.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to stay', forming an aspectual pair with 'остаться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: And the advance stays with us.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'change', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Все перемены в нашей жизни к лучшему.
examples.trans: All changes in our life are for the better.

examples.text: Ты не сможешь остановить эти важные перемены.
examples.trans: You will not be able to stop these important changes.

examples.text: И всё-таки перемены всегда неожиданно происходят.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'full' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('complete, total, utter') (полный кошмар = a total nightmare) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: На столе стоял полный стакан воды.
examples.trans: A full glass of water stood on the table.

examples.text: Ну что я тебе скажу, Аркаша? Это полный кошмар!
examples.trans: Well, what can I tell you, Arkasha? This is a total nightmare!

получать.gloss: to receive, to get; to earn

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'лучать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to receive, to get; to earn', paired with 'получить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to earn (a salary)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: А почему нет? Продавец получает больше, чем преподаватель.
examples.trans: Why not? A sales assistant earns more than a lecturer.

meanings.en: at times, sometimes, now and then
meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at times'.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся в своей правоте.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize we were right.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся, что были правы.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize that we were right.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'constantly'.

examples.trans: What are you constantly afraid of?
He was constantly late for work.
What are you constantly afraid of, Kostik?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'right', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('right, correct') (short form: ты прав = you're right) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

meanings.note: regularly, or as a general invitation: приходи!

examples.trans: If you change your mind, come back. The job is waiting.

meanings.en: to happen, take place, go on
meanings.note: Что происходит? = What is going on?

examples.trans: What is going on? I don't understand.

examples.text: Мы не знаем, что с нашей дочерью происходит!
examples.trans: We don't know what is happening with our daughter!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'earlier'.

examples.text: В моей комнате раньше дядя Миша жил.
examples.trans: Uncle Misha used to live in my room.
There used to be an old park here.

examples.text: Подождите. В моей комнате раньше дядя Миша жил.
examples.trans: Wait. Uncle Misha used to live in my room.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'next to'.
Secondary conversational sense ('nearby, close by') (adverb of place) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: A plot next to Grigory Soprykin.
Right nearby, round the corner, there's a cheburek café.

складываться.gloss: to turn out, develop, take shape

meanings.en: to take shape, turn out, form
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'кладываться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to turn out, develop, take shape', paired with 'сложиться'.

examples.text: Всё складывается даже лучше наших планов.
examples.trans: Everything is turning out even better than our plans.

examples.text: Но часто всё складывается даже лучше.
examples.trans: But often everything turns out even better.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'нова').

examples.text: Нормально? Она через неделю снова потечёт!
examples.trans: Fine? It'll be leaking again in a week!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'quite'.
Secondary conversational sense ('not at all') (совсем не) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: That's not what I mean at all.

examples.text: Нет, Вика, я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: No, Vika, that's not what I mean at all.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'old', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('former, old') ('старый друг' = an old friend) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Славик, смотри сюда. Меняю свой новый айфон на твой старый телефон.
examples.trans: Slavik, look here. I'll swap my new iPhone for your old phone.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to lose', forming an aspectual pair with 'потерять'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to waste (time)') (терять время) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Вы зря теряете время. Шпионить для вас я не буду.
examples.trans: You're wasting your time. I'm not going to spy for you.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('that') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in 'то, что ...' = 'what, the thing that'
Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common feminine noun meaning 'point, dot, spot' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: We arrived at the starting point.

examples.text: А бывает, мы приходим в исходную точку.
examples.trans: And sometimes we arrive back at the starting point.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.en: to become convinced, make sure, realize
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'беждаться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to become convinced', forming an aspectual pair with 'убедиться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: Мы убеждаемся в этом каждый день.
examples.trans: We become convinced of this every day.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся, что были правы.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize that we were right.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'дачно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Да, наш вечер закончился очень удачно.
examples.trans: Yes, our evening ended very successfully.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: О, это, Аркашенька, бывает очень часто.
examples.trans: Oh, that happens very often, Arkashenka.
We often meet in the park.
I used to come see you often.

meanings.note: the plural is a different word: люди, людям, о людях
Secondary conversational sense ('people') (plural люди, a different word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
